mainTopic: How partners with unequal investments split profit (שמואל, רבה, רב המנונא), and the order and oaths when several wives collect their כתובות.
overview: The עמוד opens with the end of שמואל's ruling: when two partners put unequal money into a shared purse, the profit is split equally. רבה limits this to an ox bought for plowing and used for plowing. If the ox was slaughtered and sold for meat, each partner takes according to his money. רב המנונא says the profit is split equally even then. The גמרא challenges רבה from a ברייתא and answers that the ברייתא's second case, separate purchases that got mixed, is really describing the slaughtered ox. Next it challenges שמואל from our משנה, which says three partners divide gains and losses by investment. רבה בר אבוה answers that 'gain' and 'loss' there mean the coins themselves went up or down in value. A new משנה follows: when a man with four wives dies, earlier כתובות are paid first, and each wife swears to the next. The תנא קמא and בן ננס argue about whether the last wife must swear. The גמרא asks what their argument depends on, and שמואל's answer begins on the next עמוד.

steps.title: End of שמואל's ruling: the profit is split equally
steps.stepSummary: The last words of שמואל's ruling, which started on the previous עמוד: when partners invest unequal sums, the profit is divided equally.
steps.simpleTranslation: The profit is split down the middle.
steps.whatsHappening: These are the closing words of שמואל's ruling from just before this point. Two partners put unequal money (one a מנה, one two hundred) into a shared purse, and the profit is split equally.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though one partner put in twice as much, שמואל rules that the earnings are divided half and half. Everything that follows in this section is about when this surprising rule applies.

keyTerms.meaning: to the middle, meaning split equally

steps.whatToRemember: Base rule (שמואל): unequal investment, but equal split of the profit.

phrases.english: the profit is divided equally.
phrases.notes: This finishes שמואל's ruling, just before this line, about two partners who invested a מנה and two hundred.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ruling of שמואל from the previous עמוד.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Partners with unequal investments split the profit equally.

steps.title: רבה limits שמואל's rule to an ox used for plowing
steps.stepSummary: רבה says שמואל's rule makes sense only when the ox was bought for plowing and used for plowing. If it was slaughtered, each partner takes according to his money.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: שמואל's statement makes sense when the ox was bought for plowing and is used for plowing. But if it was bought for plowing and ended up slaughtered, each one takes according to the money he put in.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה explains where שמואל's equal-split rule applies and where it does not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A plowing ox only works as a whole animal, so each partner's share is equally needed and the profit is split equally. Once the ox is slaughtered and sold as meat, it can be divided by weight and value. So the money is split according to how much each partner invested.

keyTerms.meaning: it makes sense, it stands to reason

phrases.english: Rabba said: Shmuel's statement makes sense
with an ox bought for plowing and used for plowing,
but with an ox bought for plowing that ends up for slaughter,
this one takes according to his money
and that one takes according to his money.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: Equal split only for an ox used for plowing. If slaughtered, the split follows each partner's investment.

steps.title: רב המנונא: equal split even if the ox was slaughtered
steps.stepSummary: רב המנונא disagrees with רבה and applies שמואל's equal split even when the plowing ox was slaughtered.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב המנונא said: even with an ox bought for plowing that ends up slaughtered, the profit is split equally.
steps.whatsHappening: A second אמורא gives the opposite view. He says שמואל's rule covers the slaughter case too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רב המנונא, what matters is how the ox was bought: as a plowing ox, a single working unit. Since that is how they bought it, the equal split stays even if they later slaughtered it.

phrases.english: And Rav Hamnuna said:
even an ox bought for plowing that ends up for slaughter,
the profit is divided equally.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רבה's limit on שמואל's rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Equal split even when a plowing ox is slaughtered.

steps.title: Challenge to רבה from a ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that partners who put unequal amounts into a purse split the profit equally. The גמרא suggests it means the slaughter case, which would refute רבה.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged this from a ברייתא: two people put money into a purse, one a מנה and one two hundred, and the profit is split equally. Isn't it talking about an ox bought for plowing that ended up slaughtered? Then it refutes רבה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that gives an equal split without saying anything about plowing. It tries to read it as covering the slaughter case, against רבה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא gives no limit, so it seems to include even the case where the ox was slaughtered. If so, it backs רב המנונא and disproves רבה.

phrases.english: They challenged from a teaching:
two who put money into a purse,
phrases.notes: Putting money into a purse means going into business together.

phrases.english: this one a maneh and that one two hundred,
the profit is divided equally.

phrases.aramaic: מַאי לָאו, בְּשׁוֹר לַחֲרִישָׁה וְעוֹמֵד לִטְבִיחָה,
phrases.english: Isn't it talking about an ox for plowing that ends up for slaughter,
and so it is a refutation of Rabba?

steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's ruling that a slaughtered ox is split by investment.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא gives an equal split with no limit, so it seems to include the slaughter case.

steps.title: The ברייתא is about an ox used for plowing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא is talking only about an ox used for plowing, which רבה agrees with.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is talking about an ox bought for plowing and used for plowing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבה by limiting the ברייתא to the plowing case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the plowing case רבה also says the profit is split equally. So the ברייתא does not contradict him.

phrases.english: No, it is about an ox for plowing that is used for plowing.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case of the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא covers even a slaughtered ox.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא covers only an ox used for plowing.

steps.title: Then why didn't the ברייתא split its own case?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back. If the ברייתא would split a slaughtered ox by investment, it could have said so about its own case instead of teaching a different case in the סיפא.
steps.simpleTranslation: But with an ox for plowing that ended up slaughtered, what would the ruling be? Each one takes according to his money? If so, instead of teaching the סיפא, 'If each one bought with his own money and the animals got mixed together, each one takes according to his money,' it should have taught the slaughter case.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer of step 5. If the ברייתא agreed with רבה, it would have taught the slaughter case as its 'each by his money' ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא does give an 'each by his money' ruling, but only in the סיפא, where each partner bought separately and the animals got mixed. It would have been simpler to split its own purse case into plowing and slaughter. Since it did not, it seems not to agree with רבה. The challenge is spelled out further in the next lines.

keyTerms.meaning: the later clause of a teaching

steps.confusionAlert: This challenge is only half-stated here. The next step finishes it by spelling out how the ברייתא should have split its own case, and step 8 answers it.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל שׁוֹר לַחֲרִישָׁה וְעוֹמֵד לִטְבִיחָה מַאי —
phrases.english: But an ox for plowing that ends up for slaughter, what would the ruling be?

phrases.aramaic: זֶה נוֹטֵל לְפִי מְעוֹתָיו וְזֶה נוֹטֵל לְפִי מְעוֹתָיו.
phrases.english: This one takes according to his money and that one takes according to his money?
Instead of teaching the later clause:
if this one bought with his own money and that one with his own money
and they got mixed together,
this one takes according to his money,
and that one takes according to his money,

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲבָל שׁוֹר לַחֲרִישָׁה וְעוֹמֵד לִטְבִיחָה מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the ברייתא covers only an ox used for plowing.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the slaughter case were split by investment, the ברייתא should have split its own case that way. Instead it taught the separate mixed-animals case in the סיפא.

steps.title: The wording the ברייתא should have used
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא spells out how the ברייתא should have been worded if it agreed with רבה: split the plowing case equally, but split the slaughter case by investment.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let the ברייתא make the distinction inside its own case: 'When is this said? When the ox was bought for plowing and used for plowing. But if it was bought for plowing and used for slaughter, each partner takes according to his money!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the challenge from step 6. It writes out the exact sentence the ברייתא should have said if רבה were right.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the ברייתא held like רבה, the easiest way to teach it would be to split its own ox case into two: plowing means an equal split, and slaughter means a split by money. Since the ברייתא did not word it that way, it seems to mean equal split in every case. That would go against רבה.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it distinguish, meaning split the case into two parts
In what case are these words said? (a formula that limits a rule)
Set aside for slaughter, meaning used for its meat

phrases.english: Let it distinguish and teach within its own case:
In what case are these words said?
With an ox bought for plowing and used for plowing.
But with an ox bought for plowing and used for slaughter —
this one takes according to his money
and that one takes according to his money!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the challenge of step 6 by writing out the ideal wording.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer in step 5 that the ברייתא is only talking about a plowing ox, which defends רבה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the ברייתא agreed with רבה, it would have drawn the plowing/slaughter line inside its own case. Since it didn't, it seems to hold an equal split everywhere.

steps.title: The ברייתא does make this distinction
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא does say exactly this. Its second case, partners who each bought separately and then mixed, describes the slaughtered ox.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is indeed what it is saying: 'When is this said? With an ox bought for plowing and used for plowing. But if it was bought for plowing and used for slaughter, it is as if each partner bought with his own money and the purchases got mixed, so each takes according to his money.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. It says the ברייתא really does make the distinction that step 7 asked for.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The second case in the ברייתא is not a separate topic. It explains the slaughter case. Once the ox is slaughtered, it is treated like two people who each bought with their own money and then mixed their goods, so each takes what his money bought. This keeps the ברייתא in line with רבה.

keyTerms.meaning: That is indeed what it is saying
According to his money, meaning in proportion to what he invested

steps.whatToRemember: According to this answer the ברייתא matches רבה. A plowing ox is split equally. A slaughtered ox is treated like separately bought goods that got mixed, so it is split by investment.

phrases.english: That is indeed what it is saying:
In what case are these words said?
With an ox bought for plowing and used for plowing.
But with an ox bought for plowing and used for slaughter —
it becomes like a case where this one bought with his own money
and that one with his own money, and they got mixed,
phrases.notes: This is the ברייתא's second case from step 6. The גמרא is saying it explains the slaughter case and is not a separate topic.

phrases.english: this one takes according to his money
and that one takes according to his money.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 7 by saying the ברייתא's second case is the very distinction that was demanded.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reading the text differently: the second case explains the first case and is not a new topic
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא's second case is a separate case, so the ox case must mean an equal split even after slaughter.
steps.terutzMaskana: The second case is the slaughter case, described as separate purchases that got mixed, so it is split by investment, just like רבה says.

steps.title: Challenge to שמואל from the three partners in the משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes our משנה: three people who put unequal money into a purse divide gains and losses by investment. It suggests this means real business profit and loss, which goes against שמואל's equal split.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned in the משנה: 'And similarly, three who put money into a purse, whether they lost or gained, divide in this way.' Isn't it that 'lost' means a real loss and 'gained' means a real gain?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new challenge, this time against שמואל himself. It brings a line from our משנה and reads it as real business profit and loss.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says the partners divide 'in this way', meaning by how much each put in. If 'lost or gained' means actual business losses and profits, then profit is split by investment and not equally. That goes against שמואל, who says profit is split equally.

keyTerms.meaning: They put money into a shared purse, meaning they invested together
Is it not? (introduces a suggested reading that sets up a challenge)

steps.confusionAlert: This challenge is aimed at שמואל, not רבה. The question is whether real profit is ever split by investment.

phrases.english: We learned in the משנה:
And similarly, three who put money into a purse,
whether they lost or gained —
this is how they divide,
phrases.notes: "This is how" means according to how much each one put into the purse.

phrases.english: Is it not:
"they lost" means they really lost,
"they gained" means they really gained!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defending רבה, the גמרא turns to a new challenge against שמואל from the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's rule that partners who invested unequally split the profit equally
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה says the partners divide by investment whether they lost or gained. If that means real business profit, then profit is split by investment, which goes against שמואל.

steps.title: Gained and lost means the coins themselves changed value
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר אבוה answers for שמואל: 'gained' means they ended up with new, better coins, and 'lost' means some coins became worn-out and nearly worthless.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said in the name of רבה בר אבוה: No. 'They gained' means they received new coins. 'They lost' means they received old coins good only for putting on a wound.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from Step 9. The purse משנה is not talking about business profit and loss.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge assumed that 'gained' and 'lost' in the משנה meant trading profit, which would go against שמואל's equal split. רבה בר אבוה explains that the משנה means the coins themselves went up or down in value. Splitting by investment applies to the coins they hold, so שמואל's rule about real profits still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: They gained, ended up with more
They lost, ended up with less
New coins, worth more than the old ones
A worn-out coin, good only for laying on a wound

steps.whatToRemember: The purse משנה's 'gain and loss' is about coins changing value, not business profit. That is how שמואל's equal split survives the challenge.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבוּהּ:
phrases.english: Rav Nachman said that Rabba bar Avuh said:
No, "they gained" means new coins,
"they lost" means a coin for a wound.
phrases.notes: An old, spoiled coin is worthless as money. The only use left for it is putting it on a wound.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבוּהּ: לָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from the purse משנה in Step 9
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the words of the משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Gained' and 'lost' meant business profit and loss, which would be split by investment against שמואל
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Gained' and 'lost' refer to the coins changing value, so business profit can still be split equally as שמואל says

steps.title: Four wives collect in order, each swearing to the next
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה: when a man with four wives dies, earlier wives collect first, and each swears to the one after her. The תנא קמא and בן ננס argue whether the last wife must also swear.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a man married to four wives dies, the first wife collects before the second, the second before the third, and the third before the fourth. The first swears to the second, the second to the third, and the third to the fourth, but the fourth is paid without an oath. בן ננס says: Should she gain just because she is last? She too is paid only with an oath.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins about the order in which several wives collect their כתובות from their husband's estate, and about who must swear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An earlier כתובה comes first, so the first wife is paid before the others. Each wife swears to the next one because if she took more than she was owed, the next wife would get less. The fourth wife has no wife after her, so the תנא קמא lets her collect without an oath. בן ננס points out that she still collects from property that would otherwise go to the orphans, so she must swear too.

keyTerms.meaning: Comes first, has the earlier right to be paid

steps.confusionAlert: Order matters here: an earlier wife always collects first. The oath goes 'down the line' to the next wife, because she is the one who would lose if the earlier wife took too much.

phrases.english: MISHNAH:

phrases.aramaic: מִי שֶׁהָיָה נָשׂוּי אַרְבַּע נָשִׁים וָמֵת —
phrases.english: One who was married to four wives and died:
the first comes before the second,
and the second before the third, and the third before the fourth.
And the first swears to the second,
and the second to the third, and the third to the fourth,
and the fourth is paid without an oath.
Ben Nanas says:
Just because she is last, should she gain?

phrases.aramaic: אַף הִיא לֹא תִּפָּרַע אֶלָּא בִּשְׁבוּעָה.
phrases.english: She too is paid only with an oath.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי שֶׁהָיָה נָשׂוּי אַרְבַּע נָשִׁים וָמֵת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה on a new topic
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Earlier wives collect first, and each swears to the next. The תנא קמא exempts the last wife from an oath, while בן ננס requires one.

steps.title: Same day or same hour: which wife comes first
steps.stepSummary: If the כתובות were written on the same day, even one hour earlier gives priority. If they were written in the same hour and there is little money, the wives split equally.
steps.simpleTranslation: If all the כתובות were written on the same day, whichever came before the other even by one hour wins. That is why in Jerusalem they used to write the hour. If they were all written in the same hour and there is only a מנה, they split it equally.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues and explains how to decide who comes first when the כתובות were written very close together.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being first depends on when each כתובה was written, down to the hour. Jerusalem's practice of writing the hour on documents made this possible to prove. When there is truly no difference in time, no wife comes first, so they share what is there equally.

keyTerms.meaning: She has won the right to be paid first
A sum of one hundred זוז

steps.whatToRemember: An earlier כתובה wins, even by one hour. With no time difference at all, the wives split equally.

phrases.english: If they all came out on one day,
phrases.notes: 'They' are the כתובות: all four were written and signed on the same day.

phrases.english: whichever comes before her fellow
even by one hour, has won.
And so in Jerusalem they would write the hours.
If they all came out in one hour,
and there is only a maneh there,
they divide equally.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה by defining what 'first' means
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Priority goes by the hour a כתובה was written. If they were written in the same hour, the wives divide equally.

steps.title: What is the real argument between the first opinion and בן ננס
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the תנא קמא and בן ננס are actually arguing about, and begins quoting שמואל's answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: About what do they argue? שמואל said:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens its discussion of the משנה by asking for the reason behind the dispute over the fourth wife's oath. This step sets up שמואל's answer, which comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides agree that the earlier wives swear to the later ones. The question is why the תנא קמא exempts the fourth wife and בן ננס does not. שמואל is about to explain the point the dispute depends on.

phrases.english: GEMARA:
About what do they argue?
phrases.notes: 'They' are the תנא קמא and בן ננס, who argue about whether the fourth wife swears.

phrases.english: Shmuel said:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא on the new משנה by asking about the dispute in Step 11
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The underlying point of disagreement between the תנא קמא and בן ננס about the fourth wife's oath
